doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Rock, fusion and smooth jazz changing the jazz scene
summary: She recalls rock like Bill Haley and Chubby Checker casting a cloud over jazz, and they discuss Bitches Brew, Weather Report and the smooth saxophone sound.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah, that’s amazing. That is very much so, some analysis like that. I was thinking . . . let’s say . . . let’s move into some of the period when jazz did get . . . evolve . . . instead of going more avant garde, it took another right angle. The music started to be more affected by rhythm-and-blues, soul music, pop music, and came a title what they call “fusion.” Did that have an impact on your playing? I think it had an impact on the industry, which we can talk about it too. But let’s talk about those groups.
I’m not sure when that happened, because I . . . for a minute I thought you were going back to that period when suddenly it seemed like rock took over.

Suddenly it was Bill Haley and the Comets, and it was Chubby Checker and all these people. It seemed like there was a cloud over jazz, because of these people. Fusion . . . I can’t exactly know when I started to hear . . . I don’t exactly know . . . I get mixed up. I don’t know what to call fusion. It’s . . . Where does a guy like Archie Shepp fit into this?
No, I would say he would be probably part of that school of John Coltrane, Cecil Taylor. Maybe I could suggest, for instance when Miles’s groups, with the Bitches Brew group . . .
Oh yeah, Bitches Brew and all those things.
. . . or when, or John McLaughlin’s group, with Tony Williams’s Lifetime . . .
. . . Return to Forever, Weather Report. That period.

Right. O.k. I guess I got to thinking of somebody whose name I can’t come up with and I know it very well . . . they started . . . this is more into WQEW, the generic saxophone sound that everybody suddenly started to get.
Oh yeah. That’s that sort of wimpy smooth jazz things.

Actually, what I wanted . . . I think what I’d like to have you answer that along those lines, is that, how did that . . . because of the shifts in the groups there . . . how did that affect you in terms of venues or places to work, concerts? How did it affect other musicians that played the style, played what we call the real deal? Did that, because there were less places to play, were there . . . did that take away . . . we knew it took away from it musically, but economically how did that affect the scene?
I’m trying to think, is it . . . did . . . when this happened. Was this in the late . . .
This is the late ’60s or early ’70s . . .
